content: The majority of hospitalized patients worldwide require the placement of a vascular access device (VAD). In the United States alone, hundreds of millions of VADs are inserted annually, and globally, over a billion peripheral intravenous catheters are used each year. Evidence suggests that utilizing a team-based approach for the assessment, insertion, and maintenance of VADs can lead to improved clinical outcomes, enhanced patient experiences, and more efficient healthcare processes. The objective of this review was to compare the effectiveness of vascular access specialist teams (VAST) with a generalist model for VAD insertion and care. The comparison focused on outcomes such as successful device insertion, prevention of device failure, and cost-effectiveness. VAST refers to a dedicated team of healthcare professionals with advanced expertise in VAD insertion techniques, clinical care, and device management. In contrast, the generalist model involves nurses, physicians, or other healthcare providers who perform VAD-related tasks alongside other clinical responsibilities and may have less specialized training in this area. To address this objective, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and clinical trial registries was conducted on February 7, 2018. These included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, EBSCO CINAHL, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, as well as registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and others. The search aimed to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the impact of VAST on clinical outcomes. A total of 2,398 citations were identified during the search. Of these, 30 studies were deemed potentially eligible for further review based on their full text. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this systematic review. One registered clinical trial was identified as ongoing, and another study was classified as awaiting further evaluation because it had not yet been accepted for publication. The authors concluded that there is currently no published RCT evidence to either support or refute the superiority of vascular access specialist teams over the generalist model for VAD insertion and care. While VAST members possess advanced skills and knowledge specific to vascular access, the generalist model involves healthcare providers who may lack this level of specialization and must balance VAD care with other clinical duties. The findings of this review may change once the ongoing study and the study awaiting classification are published. There is a clear need for high-quality RCTs to rigorously evaluate the effectiveness of VAST in improving clinical outcomes and preventing device failure.
